modules.title: Set Up Development Environments
modules.learning_content:
In this first Git module, your focus is on setting up a reliable and consistent development environment so you can safely version, track, and collaborate on code. Key concepts to master include what Git is versus platforms like GitHub or GitLab, how Git is installed on your operating system, and how it integrates with an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) such as VS Code or IntelliJ. You will also learn the purpose of global Git configuration (username, email), SSH keys, and basic repository initialization. At this proficiency level, the goal is comfort and confidence—not speed or advanced workflows.

Start with hands-on setup. Install Git locally, confirm it works from the command line, and configure your global identity. Then install an IDE commonly used on EY engagements (Visual Studio Code is a strong default) and connect it to Git. Practice creating a local repository, opening it in your IDE, and visually identifying tracked vs. untracked files. Finally, create a GitHub account and connect it securely using SSH so you can push and pull code without repeatedly entering credentials.

Common pitfalls at this stage include skipping Git configuration (leading to commits with incorrect author names), mixing up HTTPS and SSH authentication, and relying entirely on the IDE without understanding what Git commands are doing underneath. Another frequent issue is installing Git but not adding it correctly to the system PATH, which causes terminal errors. Take time to validate each step with simple checks like `git --version` and `git status`.

In EY work, Git is foundational for collaborating on client deliverables, analytics assets, automation scripts, and application code. Many EY teams use Git-based workflows for audit tooling, consulting accelerators, and internal platforms. Being able to independently set up your environment demonstrates professionalism and readiness to contribute from day one. To demonstrate this skill, be prepared to walk a colleague through your setup, explain how your IDE connects to Git, and show a clean first commit pushed to a remote repository.

modules.title: Learn Programming Fundamentals
modules.description: Understand syntax, control flow, and core programming concepts.
modules.learning_content:
In this first JavaScript module, your focus is to build a solid foundation in programming fundamentals. Key concepts to master include basic JavaScript syntax, variables (let, const), data types (string, number, boolean), operators, and simple input/output using console.log(). You will also learn control flow concepts such as conditional statements (if/else, switch) and loops (for, while), which are essential for writing logic-driven programs.

Start by practicing small, focused coding tasks. Write simple scripts that declare variables, perform calculations, and print results to the console. Progress to decision-making logic by checking conditions (e.g., validating user input or categorizing data). These exercises should be done in a browser console or a beginner-friendly environment like JSFiddle or CodePen, which removes setup complexity and lets you focus on learning.

Common pitfalls at this stage include confusing let and const, forgetting semicolons or brackets, and misunderstanding how JavaScript handles types (for example, string vs number comparisons). Another frequent challenge is debugging logic errors in if/else statements. Get comfortable reading error messages and using console.log() to inspect variable values step by step.

At EY, JavaScript fundamentals are directly applicable to technology consulting, data visualization, automation, and front-end development work. Even non-developer roles benefit from understanding how web-based tools and dashboards are built. Demonstrating this skill at EY could include automating a small task, understanding client-facing web solutions, or collaborating more effectively with technical teams.

To demonstrate proficiency, aim to explain your code clearly, including why you chose a particular condition or loop. Share a simple JavaScript script with a colleague or manager and walk them through the logic. This shows not just coding ability, but also communication and problem-solving—key capabilities valued at EY.

modules.title: Learn Programming Fundamentals
modules.description: Understand syntax, control flow, and core programming concepts.
modules.learning_content:
In this first module, your goal is to build a solid foundation in C# by understanding core programming concepts rather than memorizing syntax. Focus on how a C# program is structured (namespaces, classes, the Main method), basic data types (int, double, string, bool), variables, and simple input/output using the console. You should also become comfortable with control flow concepts such as if/else conditions, switch statements, and basic loops (for and while). These fundamentals are essential before moving into more advanced object-oriented concepts in later modules.

To make the learning practical, write small console applications as you learn each concept. Start by creating a simple program that prints messages, performs arithmetic operations, and reacts to user input. Gradually add conditional logic (e.g., validating user input) and loops (e.g., repeating calculations). Keep your programs short and focused—each exercise should demonstrate one concept clearly. Use Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code with the .NET SDK to get familiar with professional development tools used across EY technology teams.

Common pitfalls for beginners include trying to learn everything at once, copying code without understanding it, and getting stuck on syntax errors. Pay close attention to compiler error messages—they are an important learning tool. Another frequent mistake is confusing assignment (=) with comparison (==) in conditions. Take time to understand how variables change during program execution by stepping through code with a debugger.

At EY, C# fundamentals are relevant in areas such as building internal tools, supporting .NET-based client solutions, automating data processing, and collaborating with technology teams in consulting and assurance engagements. Even if you are not a full-time developer, understanding programming basics helps you communicate effectively with engineers and assess technical risks. To demonstrate this skill, be prepared to explain simple C# programs, walk through logic step by step, and show a small working console application that solves a basic business problem (e.g., calculating costs or validating inputs).
